messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marcus was eleven when the night his uncle shattered their back door forever changed the geometry of his home. He had hidden in the overgrown magnolia grove behind the house, pressing his knees into the damp soil until the screaming finally stopped. The thick scent of cheap bourbon clung to his uncle’s coat, and the heavy oak frame had collapsed against the siding with a sound that vibrated in Marcus’s teeth for days. For years afterward, he tried deliberately to reconstruct what he had witnessed, but his mind would shut down the moment he reached for it. The recollections refused to settle into a coherent timeline, arriving instead as disconnected fragments that never quite fitted together. His inability to deliberately piece together the past left raw emotional fragments that were instantly hijacked by environmental cues, so what remained was a raw, image-less terror that sat heavy in his chest whenever the wind shifted through the pines or a heavy door caught the draft. He learned early that sitting still with the fear was unbearable, so he began to fill the silence with noise. As the years passed, Marcus discovered that keeping himself constantly surrounded by people was the only reliable way to outrun the dread. At the regional warehouse where he now spent his days sorting inventory, the automatic bay doors would slam shut with a metallic thunder that instantly sent his pulse hammering. The moment the sound hit, he reached for the small bottle of whiskey he hid in his locker, just to dampen the sudden spike in his nerves. When the chemical fog lifted and the silence crept back in, he would deliberately pick arguments with foremen over minor paperwork errors, manufacturing drama just to force himself into the center of a shouting match. He was certain that if he ever allowed himself a quiet moment alone, the unanchored fear would finally swallow him whole. The warehouse became a landscape of narrowly avoided silences and carefully measured loudnesses, where every creak and draft was measured against the old terror. The habits he had built to survive the nights eventually became the very mechanisms that trapped him. Every time he drank to steady his hands or argued to distract himself, he found his capacity to process the past steadily eroding. He would sit down to review old photographs, but the memories would retreat entirely, leaving him with only the unmodulated emotional intensity of that night without any visual anchor. Because his mind kept fleeing from the recollection, his nervous system remained on perpetual standby for the next threat. His constant need for company and his reliance on substances actually stripped away his ability to ground himself in the present, so a faint whiff of someone’s cologne or a creaking floorboard now fired off the old fear signals with unmoderated force. The more he pushed the past away, the more readily ordinary environmental cues hijacked his attention. He found himself pacing the loading dock during breaks, calling friends to keep him talking, terrified that stopping meant facing the ghosts he could not name. At seventy-nine, after a particularly vivid panic attack in the grocery store aisle triggered by the sound of a shopping cart brake, Marcus finally scheduled an appointment. He did not want to forget the past, he explained quietly to the clinician; he simply wanted to stop feeling like the ground was still giving way beneath him.
